1:
What the long war consisted of was less than it sounds. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) denies pitched battles and describes a state of hostility in which each house claimed the allegiance of the whole nation; Ish-bosheth was too weak to carry on actual war, and David was content to abide the fulfilment of the promises of the Lord in his own good time, while time worked in his favour, partly through his rival’s manifest incompetence and partly through a growing realisation that he was the divinely appointed sovereign. John Gill (reformed) reckons it five years longer and supposes it was carried on not in pitched battles, of which we read no more, but in skirmishes. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) does the arithmetic from the other end, since Ish-bosheth was probably made king at once upon Saul’s death while the other tribes did not submit to David before seven years were expired. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) asks why it was long at all when right and therefore God were on David’s side, and answers that God for wise and holy ends prolonged the conflict, which tried David’s faith and patience and made his establishment at last the more welcome.

Henry then turns the war into a figure of the inward life. The contest between grace and corruption in believers, who are sanctified but in part, may fitly be compared to what is recorded here: there is a long war between them, the flesh lusting against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, but as sanctification is carried on, corruption, like the house of Saul, grows weaker and weaker, while grace, like the house of David, grows stronger and stronger, until it comes to a perfect man.

Why the list of sons stands where it does is defended and then used against David. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) hold that it does not break the thread, as Clericus and Thenius suppose, but is appropriately introduced as practical proof of the strengthening of David’s house, and in keeping with the custom of opening a reign’s history with notices of the king’s family. Henry grants the political effect, every child whose welfare was embarked in the common safety being a fresh security given to the commonwealth, but counts the cost: it was David’s fault to multiply wives contrary to the law and a bad example to his successors, and we read not that any of these sons came to be famous, three being infamous, so that we have reason to rejoice with trembling in the building up of our families. Wesley reads one marriage as policy, contracted to secure an ally against Ish-bosheth’s party in the north while David opposed him in the south, and judges that he paid dear for making piety give place to policy, as the history of Absalom shows.

Two of the names raise questions, and the answers divide. On the second son Henry relays what the Hebrew doctors say, that his first name was Daniel, meaning God has judged me, with reference to Nabal, but that David’s enemies said it was Nabal’s son and not David’s, to confute which Providence so ordered it that as he grew he came to resemble David more than any of his children, whence the name that signifies like his father. Gill reports the same etymology but dismisses the story attached to it as a fable not worth relating. On the sixth mother the three differ again: Gill notes that she alone is called David’s wife and that the Jews take her for Michal, but objects that Michal had not yet been returned to David in Hebron; Wesley accepts the identification and explains her being named last by her having been given away to another man; Henry allows only that, though she had no child after she mocked David, she might have had one before.
7:
Whether the charge was true is left open, and the voices lean differently. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) explains why it mattered: an Eastern monarch’s harem was reckoned the property of his successor, so taking a woman from it asserted a claim to the throne. He thinks it not probable that Abner had any such design, since he was exerting himself to maintain Ish-bosheth, but the king appears to have so regarded the act, and it is that implied charge of treachery which rouses him. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) admits that whether it was so does not appear, yet suspects Abner guilty because he does not expressly deny it; and he judges it would have been Ish-bosheth’s prudence to be silent, considering how much it was his interest not to disoblige the one man who had ventured all for him. John Gill (reformed) weighs it both ways: if false, Abner had reason for his anger; if true, he thought he deserved better at such hands than to be reproved for what he might reckon a very small fault.

The insult he answers with is disputed in its grammar. Ellicott holds that the received rendering is taken from the Vulgate and is hardly possible, and that it should rather run, am I a dog’s head belonging to Judah? Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) read it the same way, as am I a dog’s head, holding with Judah, and call the figure thoroughly contemptible. Henry notices what Abner thinks the service worth, since he magnifies it as rendered against Judah, the tribe on which the crown was settled, so that in supporting Saul’s house he had acted against his conscience and his interest at once; and proud men, he adds, will not bear reproof, least of all from those they think they have obliged.

The oath Abner swears by is on no record, and all three say so. Keil and Delitzsch know of no oath by which God had promised the kingdom to David, but hold the promise of God to be in itself equivalent to an oath, since he can neither lie nor deceive, and observe that the promise was generally known in Israel. Ellicott agrees that none is recorded, and suggests that the prophetic declaration that God’s choice of David was unalterable may have been considered to have the force of one. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) turns it into an accusation: why did he not do this before, when he knew that God had given the kingdom to David, and was he not until now, by his own concession, fighting against God?

What really moved him was neither piety nor policy. Ellicott denies that he proposed it to fulfil the divine will, since his words show he had been acting in conscious opposition to it, and makes revenge the spring of the thing; though he had doubtless also become satisfied of his master’s unfitness, while his power over Israel opened the prospect of high preferment from David. The suddenness of the resolve, Ellicott adds, suggests he had already had the matter under consideration, which shows there was some ground for the reproach after all. Henry watches the man change masters: his ambition had made him zealous for Ish-bosheth and his revenge now makes him as zealous for David, for those who are slaves to their lusts have many masters, driving some one way and some another; yet while Abner serves his own lusts God by him serves his own purposes, and makes even his wrath to praise him. Clarke draws a constitutional warning from the silence that follows: miserable is the lot of a king governed by the general of his army, who may strip him of power whenever he pleases, as the fates of Charles the First and Louis the Sixteenth showed; military men, above all others, should never be entrusted with civil power.
12:
Abner’s opening question is a compliment to three readers and a boast to one. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) take it to mean, to whom does the land belong except to thee. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) reads it so too, adding that it is David’s by divine right. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) expands it into a speech: David has the best title to the government and the best interest in the people’s affections. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) allows either sense but decides for the other: who has power to bring the land into subjection to whom he will except myself? Since the question is put as the basis for a league with Abner, that is evidently what is meant, and it accords with the pride and haughtiness of his character, since he proposes a league to secure consideration for himself, and makes it the price of his influence.

The condition David attaches is justified several ways. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) puts prudence first, that David should not leave a princess in the possession of a man who might in her right have pretended to the throne, besides that she was his lawful wife and he had a right to demand her. Ellicott counts three political reasons beside the justice of the claim: the demand showed all Israel that he bore no malice against the house of Saul, the restoration would again constitute him Saul’s son-in-law and so further his claim, and it showed publicly that he could enforce his rights. Henry puts the affection first, since neither her marriage nor his own had alienated him from his first and most rightful wife. Keil and Delitzsch explain why the demand went to Ish-bosheth rather than Abner: that her return might take place in duly legal form, and it be apparent David had dealt justly with her second husband before his king.

How much sympathy that husband deserves divides them sharply. Clarke gives him most: if genuine affection did not still subsist between David and Michal it was a pity to take her from a man who had her to wife by the conjoint authority of her father and her king, though David had a legal right, she having never been divorced but taken from him by violence. Ellicott thinks him sincerely attached and supposes it returned, yet holds she was not rightfully his wife and David’s claim was prior as well as better. Henry allows him no pity: he was loth to part with her and followed her weeping, but there was no remedy and he must thank himself, for when he took her he knew another had a right to her, and usurpers must expect to resign.

The promise Abner urges on the elders is, like his oath, nowhere on record. Clarke asks where it is spoken, answers that such a promise is not extant, and suggests it may mean no more than that thus, it may be presumed, God had determined. Ellicott agrees it is not contained in so many words in the records we have, and offers two accounts: an unrecorded utterance of one of the prophets, or a reasonable inference from what had been promised and from the divine support of David hitherto. Keil and Delitzsch treat the difficulty as textual, holding the verb an evident mistake in writing for a form found in many manuscripts and in all the ancient versions. Henry supplies the reference the others cannot: when God appointed Samuel to anoint him he did in effect promise that by his hand he would save Israel, for it was to that end he was made king. On the canvassing that follows, Wesley explains why Benjamin needed separate handling, as the tribe most loath to let the kingdom go out of itself, and so placed between Judah and the rest that winning it would bring in all the others.
22:
Joab’s remonstrance is allowed a grain of honesty. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) thinks it may rest on a genuine suspicion of Abner, for which his long opposition to the divine will and his present revolt gave some ground, but finds personal enmity underneath, partly fear of being supplanted by an older and famous warrior and partly the wish to avenge his brother, so that he seeks to poison David’s mind against him. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) is astonished: Joab chides his prince and reproaches him to his face as impolitic, as if David were accountable to him, and in effect calls him a fool for trusting a man he knew came to deceive him. I know not whether to wonder more that Joab had impudence enough to give such an affront or that David had patience enough to take it; and no answer is recorded, not because David feared him as Ish-bosheth had feared Abner, but because he despised him, or because Joab had not manners enough to wait for one. John Gill (reformed) supposes he was told on entering the palace, so came before the king in a passion and flew out again without waiting to be answered.

The murder itself is reconstructed closely. Ellicott notes that the gateway was a customary place of conference in the East, so Joab waited there and drew him aside into some place of privacy; the stated reason is the blood of Asahel, but the revenge was no doubt quickened by jealousy. Of the place Abner was recalled from he observes that it is known only from Josephus, twenty stadia from Hebron, so Abner can only just have left David when Joab arrived. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) states the motive flatly, that Joab feared Abner would be made captain of the host and prevented it by murdering him under pretence of avenging his brother; the murder was one of the most unprovoked and wicked, he adds, and the same man served Amasa so a little after, being a cool-blooded and finished murderer.

Whether it was blood-avenging at all is denied four ways. Henry answers that Abner slew Asahel in open war, after a warning the young man would not take, with reluctance, and in his own defence, whereas Joab shed the blood of war in peace. Ellicott takes the strength of David’s curse as proof that the act could not be justified as the lawful avenger’s, since Abner had killed Asahel in battle, unwillingly and in self-defence; and he adds the point no one else makes, that Hebron was a city of refuge, where not even the avenger might kill without a trial. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) says the same, that Abner did it for his own necessary defence, so it was no justification of this treacherous murder. Gill explains why the curse falls on a house rather than a man: Abishai was in the secret, consenting and advising, and so an accessory, perhaps present and ready to help if needed.

The curse, and what it stood in place of, divides them. Clarke reads it as prediction rather than imprecation, since the verbs may all be rendered in the future, so that it will rest on the head of Joab: a prophetic declaration showing the displeasure of God against this execrable man. Henry puts the obvious objection: a resolute punishment of the murderer himself would better have become David than this passionate imprecation of God’s judgments upon his posterity. Ellicott agrees that David remains at fault for keeping Joab in his high position, but attributes it to an inability to punish so powerful a subject, which he sought on his death-bed to remedy by his charge to Solomon. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) record only the king’s own protest, that he and his kingdom are innocent before Jehovah for ever of the blood of Abner.
31:
The public mourning is read as a sentence passed on Joab. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) gives the reason David himself offers for it, that a prince and a great man had fallen that day in Israel, since his alliance to Saul, his place as general, his interest and his former services were enough to denominate him so; and when David could not call him a saint or a good man he said nothing of that, but gave him the praise of what was true, though he had been his enemy. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) notes that David commands it with the usual signs of rent clothes and sackcloth and lays the command especially upon Joab, who is thus required to do public penance for his act, while the king himself follows the bier as chief mourner. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) agrees that Joab was especially obliged to it, to bring him to repentance and expose him to public shame; and though walking after the corpse was against the usage of kings and might seem below David’s dignity, it was now expedient to clear himself of all suspicion of concurrence. John Gill (reformed) notices what did not happen: Joab neither fled nor was laid hold on to be brought to justice, which shows how far he was too hard for David.

The lament over him is handled as poetry. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) calls it short but very pathetic, a high strain of poetry whose measure cannot easily be ascertained. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) treat the ode as a stronger proof of innocence than either the funeral or the tears, and gloss its key word: the fool is the ungodly man according to Israelitish ideas, so the sense is that Abner had made himself guilty of no crime for which he should die like a malefactor in chains, but had been treacherously murdered. Ellicott adds the effect, that the people were moved greatly by the sight of David’s sorrow but still more by the elegy, which sums the whole circumstances in a few pregnant words.

What the free hands and feet are meant to prove is spelled out. Gill explains that binding is what is done to malefactors taken up and condemned for a crime, which was not Abner’s case, so that had he been aware of the design he might either have defended himself or, finding he had too many to deal with, have used his feet and fled. Wesley presses the point against Joab: Abner did not tamely yield himself to be bound hand and foot, nor did Joab overcome him in equal combat, nor durst he attempt him that way as a soldier of any worth would have done, but by hypocrisy and perfidiousness, whereby the vilest coward may kill the most valiant person.

The fast, the people’s verdict and the king’s own plea close the chapter. Ellicott notes that the people came urging him to eat, but he refused until the sun should be down, the usual hour for ending a fast. Keil and Delitzsch report the result, that all the people perceived his trouble and were pleased by it, and all Israel discerned that day that the death had not proceeded from the king, as many had probably supposed at first, Joab having fetched Abner back in David’s name. Clarke takes the plea of weakness at its word: David had little but the title, one tribe only under his government while the sons of Zeruiah had usurped all the power and reduced him to the shadow of royalty; and the doer of evil whose reward he leaves to God is Joab, whom he appears afraid to name. Wesley allows the excuse and withdraws it: this gave some colour to the delay, yet it was a fault that David did not punish them within some reasonable time.
